method.title: Observation
method.question: Who is involved, and what happens?

method.title: Interpretation
method.question: What is the main point for the first hearers?

method.title: Application
method.question: What does this show us about God, and how will we respond?

sessions.bridgeQuestion: What will Israel learn when one ordinary king after another fails to live up to the hope of a lasting King?
hints: Before David, Israel asks for a king like other nations. Notice the hopes behind that request.
Later, the kingdom faces division. Look for what God still preserves of his promise to David.

concordance.reason: David is called away from the sheep here. This gives a setting for God’s reminder about where his kingship began.
Both passages use the picture of planting God’s people securely. Compare the promised place and the threat of being uprooted.
Peter recalls God’s oath about a descendant on David’s throne. Notice how he uses that promise when speaking about Jesus.
Gabriel’s words return to David’s throne and a kingdom without an end. Listen for the language of this promise.
Hebrews quotes the father-and-son promise when speaking about the Son. Compare its use here with the royal promise to David.
David’s throne and an unending kingdom appear again, with justice and righteousness describing the coming ruler’s government.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: Where will such a surprising King come from?
hints: People search for guidance while distress grows. This gives a setting for the light promised in the next chapter.
Later in the chapter, both leaders and people turn away from God. Notice how deep the need for a different ruler goes.

concordance.reason: This account names the northern places taken by Assyria. It helps give historical weight to Isaiah’s words about gloom in Galilee.
Zechariah also speaks of light for people in darkness and the shadow of death. Notice where that light is meant to lead them.
The yoke, the burden and Midian return here. These shared images help us recognise the kind of oppression Isaiah has in view.
Weapons are destroyed as war comes to an end. Compare that picture with Isaiah’s burning armour and bloodstained garments.
Jeremiah also describes a Davidic ruler who brings justice and safety. Compare the ruler’s character with the titles of Isaiah’s child.
Gabriel speaks of David’s throne and a kingdom that will not end. These phrases connect his announcement with Isaiah’s hope.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: Is God’s heart only for restoring Israel?
hints: Fear and exile stand behind the promise of rescue. Read this to feel the need for a shepherd.
David begins among the sheep, away from the centre of attention. Notice another unexpected beginning.

concordance.reason: The image of a cheek struck in humiliation appears in both texts. Compare the suffering each passage describes before following Micah’s promise.
Matthew cites the Bethlehem prophecy in the search for the child. Notice how the ruler is described as a shepherd.
People recall both David’s family and Bethlehem when discussing the Christ. This shows the expectation attached to Micah’s promise.
Isaiah speaks of a remnant returning to God. Compare that hope with the brothers who return to Israel in Micah.
Strength and shepherding belong together in both passages. Notice how the powerful shepherd cares for the vulnerable.
The words about peace invite comparison: Micah says the ruler will be their peace, while Ephesians describes the peace Christ brings.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: What sign will tell us that what God promised so long ago has finally begun?
hints: Zion feels forgotten. God’s answer helps us hear restoration as hope for people in real distress.
The promise to Abraham already includes other nations. Notice how far the blessing is meant to reach.

concordance.reason: Jeremiah’s calling also begins before birth and reaches the nations. Compare the language of calling without assuming both servants have the same task.
Both passages connect the servant’s work with his speech. Notice the difference between the sharp-sword image and a word that sustains the weary.
Another servant passage speaks of God’s delight and a mission among the nations. Read the two portraits alongside one another.
Paul also fears that his labour may have been in vain. The shared concern helps us hear the servant’s discouragement, in a different setting.
Paul links Christ’s service to the confirmation of promises made to Israel’s fathers. Compare this with the servant’s task of gathering Israel.
Paul and Barnabas quote the promise of light to the nations. This is a direct link from the servant’s mission to the story in Acts.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: If John’s role is to prepare the way, who is so important that he needs such preparation?
hints: A messenger comes before the Lord, and his coming brings cleansing. This gives a setting for John’s task.
The promise speaks of hearts turning. Notice what kind of preparation the people need.

concordance.reason: Abijah appears among the priestly divisions. This small detail helps place Zechariah’s service within Israel’s ordered temple worship.
Abraham and Sarah also face old age without the promised child. Notice the shared human limitation behind these unexpected births.
The instructions for burning incense explain the temple duty Zechariah is carrying out when the messenger appears.
Malachi promises a messenger who prepares the way. This gives a background for John’s work of turning people towards the Lord.
Gabriel echoes the promise of Elijah and the turning of hearts. Compare the wording to see how John’s task is introduced.
Rachel also speaks of God taking away her reproach after giving her a child. The shared language helps us hear Elizabeth’s personal relief.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: What kind of salvation will this King actually bring when he comes?
hints: Return to the promise of a house, a kingdom and a throne. Listen for its language in Gabriel’s announcement.
A child is given as a sign in a time of fear. Compare this promise of God’s presence with Mary’s scene.

concordance.reason: The promised child and the virgin invite comparison. Read Isaiah’s sign in its own setting as you consider Luke’s account of Mary.
Matthew explains the name Jesus by speaking of salvation from sins. This adds a clue to the mission of the child Gabriel names.
The promise of David’s house and throne stands behind Gabriel’s announcement. Notice what is repeated and what is now made clearer.
Daniel also describes a kingdom that will not pass away. Compare its reach among the nations with the reign Gabriel announces.
Matthew also identifies the Holy Spirit’s work in Mary’s pregnancy. The two accounts help us compare what is said about Jesus’ birth.
The question about anything being too hard for God accompanies the promise to Sarah. It gives an earlier setting for Gabriel’s assurance.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: What will it look like when God’s King actually steps into our world?
hints: Hannah’s song celebrates God lifting the weak. Listen for images that return in Mary’s praise.
God promises a lasting relationship with Abraham’s descendants. This gives a setting for the close of Mary’s song.

concordance.reason: The earlier promise about John and the Holy Spirit prepares us for Elizabeth’s Spirit-filled response when Mary arrives.
Believing and blessing are linked in both passages. Compare Mary’s trust in God’s word with the blessing Jesus describes.
Hannah’s song also celebrates God lifting the weak and bringing down the proud. Listen for the shared movement in these two songs.
The psalm connects enduring mercy with those who fear God. These shared words place Mary’s praise within Israel’s worship.
Hannah sings of God raising the poor and bringing people low. Compare that reversal with Mary’s words about rulers and the humble.
God’s promise to Abraham names Isaac and an enduring covenant. This gives a setting for Mary’s remembrance of mercy through generations.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: If heaven sees this birth very differently from the world, who will be the first to hear heaven’s explanation of what has just happened?
hints: Bethlehem is small, yet a shepherd ruler will come from it. Keep that contrast in mind as you read Luke.
Mary has sung about the powerful and the lowly. Her words may sharpen what we notice in the birth scene.

concordance.reason: Luke uses the language of the inhabited world under another emperor. This helps us notice the wider Roman setting of the census.
Micah names Bethlehem as the place from which a ruler will come. Compare that promise with the town reached by Joseph and Mary.
Samuel is sent to Jesse in Bethlehem. This earlier scene explains the town’s connection with David’s family.
Matthew also describes Mary and Joseph’s betrothal during her pregnancy. It adds a personal setting to Luke’s brief account of their journey.
Paul speaks of Christ becoming poor for others. Compare that pattern of humility with the modest circumstances of the child’s birth.
John describes the Word becoming flesh and dwelling among us. Read this alongside Luke’s concrete details of a newborn child.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: Will the people who have waited for God to comfort Israel recognise his salvation when they see it?
hints: A child is promised whose rule brings peace. Listen for that hope in the angels’ announcement.
The call to comfort follows sorrow and guilt. This helps us hear why news of a Saviour matters.

concordance.reason: David was called from caring for sheep. The shared shepherd setting is worth noticing in a birth announced near David’s town.
Isaiah joins good news, peace, salvation and God’s reign. These words help us listen carefully to what the angel announces.
Isaiah’s promised child is given royal titles. Compare those names with the angel’s words about the child born in David’s city.
Romans speaks of peace with God through Jesus Christ. This offers another setting in which to explore the peace praised by the angels.
Jesus later sends a healed man to tell what God has done. Compare this response with the shepherds sharing what they have heard and seen.
Mary again keeps events in her heart later in the chapter. This repeated response helps us follow her place in Luke’s story.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: Who does Jesus understand himself to be?
hints: The servant’s mission reaches beyond Israel. Compare that reach with Simeon’s words about the child.
Zechariah names forgiveness, light and peace. These give shape to the salvation Simeon and Anna await.

concordance.reason: The command to circumcise a boy on the eighth day explains the timing of this scene within Israel’s covenant life.
The law allows two birds when a family cannot afford a lamb. This detail helps us understand the offering brought by Jesus’ parents.
Isaiah gives words to people who have waited for God’s salvation. Compare their joy with Simeon’s long expectation.
The servant’s mission includes light for the nations. Simeon’s words echo that hope as he holds the child.
Isaiah describes a stone over which people stumble. Compare that warning with Simeon’s words about falling and rising.
Zechariah’s song also celebrates redemption for God’s people. Anna’s words connect the temple scene with that earlier hope.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: What happens when this hidden Son steps into public view and begins his mission?
hints: Samuel also grows in favour with God and people. Compare the familiar childhood language with Jesus’ unique words about his Father.
Recall the identity announced before Jesus’ birth. His words in the temple add a new scene to that story.

concordance.reason: Samuel also grows in favour with God and people. Compare the childhood language while attending to what is distinctive about Jesus.
The command to remember Passover explains the feast that brings Jesus’ family to Jerusalem year after year.
Isaiah describes listening like a learner. Compare this picture with Jesus listening and asking questions among the teachers.
People later wonder at Jesus’ learning. This offers another scene of surprise at his understanding.
Jesus later speaks of doing the will of the One who sent him. Compare that priority with his words about his Father here.
Mary’s habit of keeping events in her heart returns from the birth scene. Notice how Luke carries her reflection through the chapter.

sessions.bridgeQuestion: What will his rule look like when he begins to confront the world as it really is?
hints: Read the prophecy Luke quotes. Notice the road being prepared and the breadth of the promised salvation.
The Spirit rests on a servant who brings justice gently. Keep this portrait in mind as Jesus’ public work begins.

concordance.reason: Paul explains John’s baptism as a call to repentance that points towards Jesus. This helps place John within the larger Luke–Acts story.
Luke quotes this prophecy directly. Reading its setting helps us hear why preparing the Lord’s way carries a promise of salvation.
Paul also connects repentance with deeds that fit it. Compare that call with the practical responses John asks for.
Sharing food and clothing is also part of Isaiah’s call to faithful living. These actions make John’s call to repentance concrete.
Jesus returns to the contrast between John’s water baptism and baptism with the Holy Spirit. This connection reaches into the opening of Acts.
God’s delight in his servant and the gift of the Spirit appear together here. Compare that portrait with the voice and the Spirit at Jesus’ baptism.
